## The idea

The distance from C to E has two coordinates. Count letter names inclusively, C–D–E, and the interval is a third. Count equal-tempered semitones and the distance is four. The letter count supplies size; the semitone count determines quality. Together they name a major third.

An *interval* therefore carries two measurements. Careful listening may suggest chromatic distance, but the program calculates it; sound cannot report how the notes were spelled. C-sharp to E and D-flat to E both span three semitones in equal temperament, yet C–D–E is a third and D–E is a second. This is the practical reason Lesson 10 kept a label beside the MIDI pitch.

The first interval-naming function handles a deliberately narrow domain: simple ascending examples whose expected forms are major or perfect. Read its result as a first join between letter space and semitone space, not as a complete theory library.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72

letters = {c: 0, d: 1, e: 2, f: 3, g: 4, a: 5, b: 6}
base_distance = {1 => 0, 2 => 2, 3 => 4, 4 => 5, 5 => 7, 6 => 9, 7 => 11, 8 => 12}

define :interval_name do |first, second, letter_map, distances|
  size = ((letter_map[second[:letter]] - letter_map[first[:letter]]) % 7) + 1
  semitones = second[:pitch] - first[:pitch]
  expected = distances[size]
  quality = semitones == expected ? ([1,4,5,8].include?(size) ? "perfect" : "major") : "altered"
  "#{quality} #{size}"
end

c = {letter: :c, pitch: note(:c4)}
e = {letter: :e, pitch: note(:e4)}
puts interval_name(c, e, letters, base_distance)
play c[:pitch]; sleep 1; play e[:pitch]
```

The program prints “major 3,” then plays C followed by E. The two notes provide the four-semitone distance; the hashes provide the letters needed to count a third. If you changed only `:letter` while retaining the numeric pitches, playback would stay the same and the calculated size would change. That separation is the central evidence of the lesson.

## Change one thing

1. Add C–F and C–F-sharp. Both pairs span the letter names C–D–E–F and therefore remain fourths. The extra semitone in F-sharp changes the quality from perfect to augmented; the current helper will report that second result as `altered`.

2. Restore the original example, then compare C-sharp–E with D-flat–E. Print both MIDI differences and letter sizes. The playback distance should coincide while the sizes differ.

3. Restore C–E and reverse the pair. Before editing the function, decide whether its output should preserve direction as a separate field or normalise the notes into an ascending interval. The choice changes the interface, so state it before changing the arithmetic.

## Why it works

Interval naming joins two coordinate systems. The `letters` hash maps seven letter names onto a cycle. Subtracting their indices modulo seven and adding one gives an inclusive ordinal size: equal letters form a unison, adjacent letters form a second, and so on. MIDI subtraction independently supplies the semitone distance.

The `base_distance` table says how many semitones an unaltered major or perfect interval of each simple size contains. Sizes 1, 4, 5, and 8 belong to the perfect family; sizes 2, 3, 6, and 7 belong to the major/minor family. The current function recognises only an exact baseline and calls every deviation `altered`. That limitation is explicit enough to guide the extension.

A full quality calculation compares the actual semitone count with the baseline. For a third, four semitones is major, three is minor, five is augmented, and two is diminished. For a fourth, five semitones is perfect, six is augmented, and four is diminished. The letter-derived family determines which quality names are available.

The pitch hashes keep the join honest. If you retained only MIDI values, the helper could calculate four semitones but would have to invent a spelling before calling the result a third. If you retained only letters, it could count a third but would not know whether the sound was major, minor, diminished, or augmented.

Compound intervals continue the inclusive letter count beyond an octave, and descending intervals add a direction policy. Both features are useful, but the first implementation remains within simple ascending pairs so its lookup and failure modes stay visible. Extend direction and compound size separately; otherwise one incorrect result may have several plausible causes.

Lesson 19 leaves calculation behind and builds perceptual records for selected distances. The name will come from this two-coordinate system, while recognition must develop from repeated melodic and harmonic hearing.

## Take it further

Extend `interval_name` to return diminished, minor, major, perfect, and augmented qualities for simple ascending intervals within an octave. Create explicitly spelled test pairs from C to every chromatic pitch you need, including enharmonic alternatives where a semitone distance can have more than one size.

For every case, assert an expected label and print the semitone distance beside it. Run those assertions as a data check, then audition representative pairs in Sonic Pi 5. A correct name proves that spelling and distance were joined according to the rules. Recognising that interval by ear is a separate ability, and it is the subject of the next lesson.
